text: Microsoft Co-Pilot is Microsoft's AI assistant that knows your work natively. It is connected to the Microsoft Graph, which is a network of organizational data, which includes your email, your calendar, your Teams conversations, even SharePoint documents and meeting recordings. The simplest way to understand Co-Pilot is that it operates in three primary modes. The first one is Co-Pilot Chat. So this is a conversational assistant, and it works very similar to JTBT, but it can also search the web and then filter by your company data. You can use it for research, for synthesis, or for quick thinking between tasks. Then there is Co-Pilot inside of Microsoft 365 apps. So think about Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook. Here it can help you write content, analyze data, create presentations, and prepare work without leaving the tool that you're already in. And then there's Co-Pilot in Teams. So for anyone in back-to-back meetings, this is often where you feel the benefit the most. You get automatic meeting summaries, follow-up drafts, and scheduling support without touching a single note, and that really feels like a real-life Jarvis. Now, in terms of features, Co-Pilot does sometimes get a bad rat, but it really does pack a ton of features. So we already talked about how Co-Pilot is available directly in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, and it's getting better and better in those apps. Then there's, as we said, Co-Pilot Search, but it also has a dedicated researcher agent which can browse hundreds of sources to give you a rich, cited report. There's an analyst agent that processes and analyzes and visualizes very complex data. There is a designer for high-quality visuals, and then with the other app called ClipChamp, you can even edit those into short videos. There's Co-Pilot Pages, which is a persistent, editable workspace that turns any Co-Pilot output into collaborative content, and there's Voice and Vision, so it can use Voice, and it can also see via screen-sharing or via your camera feed on certain devices. There is Tasks, which means that it can run multi-step jobs in the background and a more complex agent builder where you can connect external systems and publish custom agents directly into your MS 365 environment, and for admins, there's even a more advanced Co-Pilot Studio. Now, in terms of the models, Co-Pilot doesn't run its own or even just one fixed model. The current lineup includes GPT 5.5 ThinkDeper for complex reasoning, GPT 5.4 ThinkDeper for multi-step analysis, and then GPT 5.2 for the faster everyday responses. Microsoft has recently also expanded beyond OpenAI models with Cloud Opus, which is available in the model selector and also in tools like Excel. What happens behind the scenes is that often Co-Pilot will automatically route requests to whichever model it thinks it's best, which is convenient, but obviously also means that you have limited visibility and input into which model is actually doing the task for you. And so where possible for high stakes analysis, we always recommend to select manually which model you're using in something called the model picker. Now, Co-Pilot is very strong on data privacy and enterprise security. It respects all of the existing permissions, meaning that users only get access to content that you're already authorized to see as a human. And all of the data is not used to train the model and even things like tenant isolation apply. And this is exactly why so many organizations choose Co-Pilot as the quote-unquote save AI option for company use. Now, finally, in terms of plans and pricing, the free tier will give you Co-Pilot Chats only grounded in public web data. With Microsoft 365 Personal, which is $10 per month or $100 a year, you get Co-Pilot directly in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook for individual use. For organizations, if you're under 300 users, you can use Microsoft 365 Co-Pilot Business, which is $21 per user per month, currently discounted to $18 on an annual plan. And this is the tier that most of our learners are working with or making a case for. And then for larger organizations, there is Microsoft 365 Co-Pilot Enterprise, which is $30 per user per month, which adds a couple of things but is largely the same. Now, one important detail, even if your team is signed in with a work account, you only get the full Co-Pilot experience if your IT administrator has assigned you a Co-Pilot license. And without that, Co-Pilot has no app integration, no organizational context, so it's as valuable as the free Co-Pilot account.
